unconditionally. Being able to authenticate to a server is not evidence of being allowed to see what
the *owner* read from it, and the Gadget runs on the owner's credentials throughout. Writes still
work — the alternative, marking every observation `prohibitAllSharing`, would latch a lockdown that
blocks every action for the rest of the session. See
[`sharing-policy.ts`](../mcp-shared/src/sharing-policy.ts).

To share the work rather than the binding, publish the Gadget as a blueprint and let each person
connect their own server.

## Notes and current limitations

- **No simulation.** MCP describes no way to predict a tool's effect, so a queued call is not
  reflected in later reads. `awaitDecision` is set and the agent's turn suspends until the user
  decides.
- **No revert.** MCP describes no inverse for a tool call, so `implementsRevert` is false.
- **No hooks.** `notifications/tools/list_changed` is session-scoped; a Gadget hook is durable and
  must survive restarts.
- **No scoping below tool names.** MCP tools take arguments, not capabilities, so "this repo only"

- **Only `tools/*`.** Prompts, resources, sampling, and elicitation are not implemented. Sampling
  and elicitation would let a server drive the agent.
- **Tool-list changes are adopted, not pinned.** A changed list is taken and logged
  (`catalog.changed`), since refusing to see new tools would break working Gadgets. A binding with a
  tool scope cannot widen this way, which is the reason to prefer **Choose tools** for anything that
  writes.
- **SSRF is enforced after DNS, not by the blocklist.** The hostname patterns in `endpoint.ts` are a
  legible refusal at connect time; they cannot see through a public hostname that resolves, or
  rebinds, to a private address. The actual boundary is the `global_fetch_strictly_public`
  compatibility flag in `wrangler.jsonc`, which makes workerd reject reserved IP ranges after
  resolution on every request and redirect hop. It does not apply under `wrangler dev`, which is
  what keeps `MCP_ALLOW_INSECURE` usable locally.
- **Sharing UI reports late.** `GadgetMetadata.sharingProhibited` derives only from
  `prohibitAllSharing`, so creating a share key appears to succeed and fails when the recipient
  opens it. Fixing this needs a kernel change.

## Layout

| File | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `src/mcp.ts` | Vendor, account DO, user, verifier, gatekeeper facet, session |
| `src/connect-form.ts` | The endpoint prompt served during connect |
| `src/server-id.ts` | Endpoint to display slug, for the binding name and session type |
| `src/configurator/` | The grant UI (compiled into `src/generated/`) |

[`@gadgets/mcp-shared`](../mcp-shared/README.md).

pnpm --filter @gadgets/mcp-gatekeeper test:run    # vitest
```

1: # MCP Server Portals gatekeeper
2: 
3: Connects the deployment's own MCP portal as a Gadgets capability. An administrator configures one
4: URL; everyone in the organization then reaches every MCP server the organization has approved
5: through it, and no user ever types an endpoint. Runs as its own Cloudflare Worker and is
6: auto-discovered by the backend from its `GATEKEEPER_MCP_PORTAL` binding.
7: 
8: The intended deployment is a
9: [Cloudflare MCP server portal](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/):
10: Access decides who may connect, Cloudflare Gateway logs and inspects what crosses, and this
11: connector turns what is behind it into typed capabilities that Gadgets can grant one server at a
12: time.
13: 
14: For endpoints a user supplies themselves, use [`gatekeeper-mcp`](../gatekeeper-mcp/README.md).
15: 
16: ## What it provides
17: 
18: One resource type, **MCP portal server**, at two grant breadths. A grant always names one upstream
19: server; "everything the portal offers" is not offered, since it would hand a Gadget every tool of
20: every system the organization has connected in one click.
21: 
22: | Granularity | Resource URL | Session type |
23: | --- | --- | --- |
24: | **Server** — every tool of one upstream server, including ones it adds later | `<endpoint>#server=github` | `Mcp<Name><tag>Session` |
25: | **Named tools** — only the listed tools of that server | `<endpoint>#server=github&tool=github_a&tool=github_b` | `Mcp<Name><tag>Session` |
26: 
27: `<tag>` is four hex characters derived from the resource URL. It matters most here: two grants
28: pinning different tools of one upstream server share both the name and the endpoint, so the scope is
29: the only thing that distinguishes them.
30: 
31: The session API — a typed method per described tool, plus `callTool`, `getActionResult`, and
32: `listTools` with progressive search/name options — is the same as
33: [`gatekeeper-mcp`](../gatekeeper-mcp/README.md#what-it-provides).
34: 
35: A server-wide grant can cover more tools than one catalog describes, so its authority is not limited
36: to the ones with generated signatures. `listTools({ search })` searches beyond the bounded preview
37: and returns up to 20 compact matches within the shared 5,000-tool / 4 MiB discovery scan;
38: `listTools({ name })` loads one exact bounded definition, and `callTool` resolves that name under the
39: same bound before dispatch. Every path rejects names outside the
40: binding's scope before loading the catalog or contacting the endpoint. Discovery and read results are
41: recorded as observations; writes retain the ordinary approval flow.
42: 
43: Scoping to one server also shrinks what the agent reads: only that server's tools are rendered as
44: signatures, and only as many as the budget describes. Additional tools are discovered on demand
45: within the explicit scan limits above; exceeding a limit fails rather than pretending a tool is absent.
46: 
47: ## Configuration
48: 
49: | Variable | Meaning |
50: | --- | --- |
51: | `MCP_PORTAL_URL` | The portal's MCP endpoint. Unset means the connector hides itself. |
52: | `MCP_PORTAL_NAME` | Display name in the connector list and every approval prompt. Defaults to `MCP Server Portal (<host>)`. |
53: | `MCP_PORTAL_AUTH` | `oauth` (default), `none`, or `token`. |
54: | `MCP_PORTAL_TOKEN` | Secret bearer token, for `MCP_PORTAL_AUTH: "token"`. |
55: | `MCP_PORTAL_TRUST_ANNOTATIONS` | `true` to let upstream tool annotations drive auto-approval. Off by default; see below. |
56: | `MCP_PORTAL_HIDDEN_SERVER_IDS` | Comma-separated upstream server IDs to hide from the configurator and refuse at the grant boundary. |
57: | `MCP_ALLOW_INSECURE` | `"true"` to disable the endpoint checks entirely: permits `http://` **and** private, loopback, link-local, and cloud-metadata hosts, for the portal and every OAuth URL discovered from it. Local dev only. |
58: 
59: The portal must expose upstream tools directly. Use a portal where Code Mode is off or opt-in, or
60: append `?codemode=off` when its policy is default-on. Enforced Code Mode is unsupported. Do not add
61: an `optimize_context` parameter or opt in to Code Mode on `MCP_PORTAL_URL`.
62: 
63: Only `MCP_ALLOW_INSECURE` is set in the repo's `wrangler.jsonc`, pinned to `"false"` so the default
64: is explicit rather than merely absent. None of the others is, and a portal URL committed there would
65: become the default for every deployment of this repo and would send their users' OAuth flows to
66: whichever host it named, so it belongs in the deployment's own configuration — for Cloudflare's
67: internal deployment, the per-package overrides in `gadgets-internal`.
68: 
69: Unconfigured, `getSupportedResources()` returns nothing and the Workshop drops the vendor. A
70: `MCP_PORTAL_URL` that cannot be used — a non-`https` typo or a URL containing `username:password`,
71: say — is treated the same way, so a misconfiguration hides the connector rather than producing one
72: that fails on first use or copying URL credentials into account state and configurator fields.
73: 
74: Changing `MCP_PORTAL_URL` on a deployment that already has connected accounts is a **repoint**.
75: Existing bindings fail closed at once: the minting path checks facet props against current
76: configuration, and an already-minted facet must name its endpoint when asking the account for
77: credentials, which the account refuses after it has moved. The user recovers by reconnecting, which
78: is the one endpoint change an account will accept. It is accepted only because the new endpoint
79: comes from this Worker's configuration rather than from a form. Nothing held for the old portal
80: survives the move: tokens, the transport session, and any in-progress authorization are dropped, so
81: the user re-authorizes against the new host. The account advances a persisted generation before
82: probing; refreshes, expiry notifications, and session writes that started under the old generation
83: are ignored when they eventually return. Always-approve action kinds also include the exact endpoint,
84: so consent for the old portal does not carry over to the new one.
85: 
86: `MCP_PORTAL_TRUST_ANNOTATIONS` is read at each point of use (`portalTrust(env)`) and never
87: persisted on an account or a binding's props, so clearing it de-escalates every existing connection
88: on the next call. Setting it does not retroactively auto-apply anything; the user must still enable
89: a rule for each action kind.
90: 
91: ## How the connect flow works
92: 
93: There is no connect form: the endpoint is a deployment setting, so pressing "connect" goes straight
94: to the portal's own sign-in. Under `MCP_PORTAL_AUTH: "oauth"` the gatekeeper runs the same
95: discovery chain as [`gatekeeper-mcp`](../gatekeeper-mcp/README.md#how-the-connect-flow-works)
96: against the portal; under `"token"` it presents `MCP_PORTAL_TOKEN` and no user interaction is
97: needed; under `"none"` it connects unauthenticated.
98: 
99: The account records `provenance: "deployment"`, which is what keeps an upstream server from renaming
100: itself over `MCP_PORTAL_NAME` in every approval prompt.
101: 
102: ## Granting
103: 
104: The configurator asks which server behind the portal, how broad the grant is, and — if it is
105: pinned — which tools:
106: 
107: ```
108: Server · Which server behind this portal to grant. Its tools appear next.
109: [ 🔍 GitHub ]
110: 
111: Tools · Choose how much of this server the Gadget may call.
112: (•) All tools      Every tool this server offers, including ones it adds later.
113: ( ) Choose tools   Only the tools you tick. Anything else is refused, including tools added later.
114: 
115: Allowed tools · Read-only tools return data straight away. The rest queue for your approval.
116: [ 🔍 Filter tools... ]
117: 12 of 12 selected                                                                     Clear
118: ☑ List issues                                                                     read-only
119: ☑ Create issue                                                               needs approval
120: ```
121: 
122: **All tools** is the default. The breadth is asked outright rather than inferred from whether every
123: box is ticked, since the two look identical and diverge as soon as the server publishes another
124: tool. A portal with one server behind it collapses to the tool questions alone, because the choice
125: is made for the user rather than skipped — the grant still records that server.
126: 
127: Every grant here names exactly one upstream server. There is no breadth that spans the portal, so a
128: configured endpoint with no upstream servers — a plain MCP server, or a portal that currently fronts
129: nothing — is **not grantable through this connector**: the configurator has no server to offer and
130: the form stays unsubmittable. That is deliberate. The alternative is a grant recorded against the
131: bare endpoint, which would silently include every server added to it later. Point a plain MCP
132: endpoint at the **MCP** connector (`gatekeeper-mcp`) instead, which is built for exactly that and
133: offers endpoint-wide and per-tool grants.
134: 
135: ## How upstream servers are recovered
136: 
137: A portal flattens every upstream server's tools into one `tools/list`, so the seam has to be
138: recovered from two facts in the portal's documented contract:
139: 
140: 1. Every tool is named `{server_id}_{original_name}`, split on the first underscore only, and an
141:    alias replaces the tool name but never the server-id prefix. Membership is therefore a pure
142:    string test needing no network call, so a server scope cannot fail open on a transient error.
143: 2. `portal_list_servers` is available in every portal session and returns each upstream server's id,
144:    name, and enabled state.
145: 
146: Detection is a capability probe — does the endpoint offer `portal_list_servers`? — not a hostname
147: match, so it works for a custom portal hostname and for any other aggregator adopting the
148: convention. A *truncated* listing counts as a portal whether or not the probe tool is in it:
149: `tools/list` is unordered, so concluding "not a portal" because the evidence fell past the cut would
150: fail open on the `portal_*` exclusion below. Truncation is reported by the client rather than
151: inferred from the tool count, because either cap can stop a listing — the count the caller asked for,
152: or the 96 KiB UTF-8 budget, and the latter can cut a listing of verbose tools short while leaving an
153: array that looks complete. The byte budget leaves 32 KiB below Durable Object's per-value limit for
154: the cache wrapper and serialization overhead; if storage nevertheless rejects the cache value, the
155: fresh catalog is still used for that operation rather than turning a cache miss into a failure.
156: 
157: ### Surveying a portal too large for one catalog
158: 
159: The configurator normally gets server names directly from `portal_list_servers`, without surveying
160: every upstream tool. If that response is unavailable or only partly understood, it falls back to a
161: **name-only tool index** of up to 1,000 entries. The index detects the portal and recovers server
162: membership from tool-name prefixes; it carries no descriptions, schemas, or policy claims, so the
163: 96 KiB result budget covers as many names as possible. A truncated fallback cannot establish the
164: complete server list and blocks the form rather than presenting a partial list as complete.
165: 
166: After a server is selected, a separate filtered scan returns up to 200 compact summaries from that
167: server. Each summary carries its bounded title, description, and annotations, and is classified
168: through the shared `tools.ts` trust boundary before it becomes a read-versus-approval label. The
169: filter is applied before result budgets, so unrelated servers cannot crowd the selected one out.
170: Only the returned prefix is offered for an individual-tool grant; additional tools require the
171: server-wide grant, and a call resolves the full definition before approval or dispatch.
172: 
173: Index entries are typed separately (`IndexedTool`) to distinguish name-only survey results from tool
174: definitions rendered into approval prompts or handed to an agent.
175: 
176: The server list is advisory: it supplies display names and ordering while tool-name prefixes remain
177: the authority on membership, and a failed call degrades to bare ids recovered from tool prefixes.
178: The gatekeeper makes that call
179: while building a form, so it does not pass through the approval queue. Failing to reach the portal
180: at all is different, and blocks the grant rather than falling back to the bare endpoint — the
181: configurator reports it and stays unsubmittable.
182: 
183: `portal_*` tools are excluded from every grant at every scope. `portal_toggle_servers` and friends
184: change which upstream servers the session can reach, so granting one would let a Gadget widen its
185: own authority. This is a capability-boundary rule, not a policy preference, and is not configurable.
186: 
187: ## Approvals and sharing
188: 
189: Identical to [`gatekeeper-mcp`](../gatekeeper-mcp/README.md#approvals-and-sharing), except for the
190: trust tier. A portal is an aggregator: `destructiveHint` and `idempotentHint` are written by
191: whichever upstream server it fronts, servers the administrator who chose the portal never reviewed,
192: and any one of them could self-declare both and get writes that skip the approval prompt. So the
193: tier is `byo` unless a deployment sets `MCP_PORTAL_TRUST_ANNOTATIONS=true`. That flag is the
194: "trusted server" assertion MCP's guidance asks for, and it has to be about the upstreams themselves,
195: not just the portal in front of them.
196: 
197: `addObserver` refuses everyone, as it does for user-supplied endpoints. Reaching the portal is not
198: the same as being allowed to see a particular tool result, and the Gadget runs on the owner's
199: credentials regardless. A sharper check is available here than for a bare endpoint —
200: `portal_list_servers` is per-user and Access-filtered, so it could confirm a collaborator may reach
201: the same server — but that is still server-granular, not record-granular. See
202: [`sharing-policy.ts`](../mcp-shared/src/sharing-policy.ts).
203: 
204: ## Notes and current limitations
205: 
206: The limitations in
207: [`gatekeeper-mcp`](../gatekeeper-mcp/README.md#notes-and-current-limitations) apply here too: no
208: simulation, no revert, no hooks, no scoping below tool names, and `tools/*` only. SSRF is enforced
209: the same way, by `global_fetch_strictly_public` rather than by hostname patterns. In addition:
210: 
211: - **One portal per deployment.** `MCP_PORTAL_URL` is a single value; a second portal needs a
212:   second Worker.
213: - **Server ids come from tool-name prefixes.** An aggregator that flattens tools without prefixing
214:   them exposes no upstream seam, so this connector finds no server to scope a grant to and the form
215:   stays unsubmittable. It is not granted as a whole endpoint — that grant does not exist here. Use
216:   the **MCP** connector (`gatekeeper-mcp`) for such an endpoint, where endpoint-wide breadth is an
217:   explicit, reviewable choice.
218: 
219: ## Layout
220: 
221: | File | Purpose |
222: | --- | --- |
223: | `src/portal.ts` | Vendor, account DO, user, gatekeeper facet, session, configurator RPC |
224: | `src/config.ts` | Reading and validating the deployment's portal configuration |
225: | `src/configurator/` | The grant UI (compiled into `src/generated/`) |
226: 
227: Everything else comes from [`@gadgets/mcp-shared`](../mcp-shared/README.md).
228: 
229: ## Build & test
230: 
231: ```
232: pnpm exec vp run -F @gadgets/mcp-portal-gatekeeper build   # build:configurator + tsc
233: pnpm --filter @gadgets/mcp-portal-gatekeeper test:run    # vitest
234: ```
235: 
236: The Worker is run via the root `pnpm dev-server`, not directly.

(End of file - total 236 lines)

# MCP Server Portals gatekeeper

auto-discovered by the backend from its `GATEKEEPER_MCP_PORTAL` binding.

The intended deployment is a
[Cloudflare MCP server portal](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/):
Access decides who may connect, Cloudflare Gateway logs and inspects what crosses, and this

time.

For endpoints a user supplies themselves, use [`gatekeeper-mcp`](../gatekeeper-mcp/README.md).

## What it provides

One resource type, **MCP portal server**, at two grant breadths. A grant always names one upstream
server; "everything the portal offers" is not offered, since it would hand a Gadget every tool of
every system the organization has connected in one click.

| Granularity | Resource URL | Session type |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Server** — every tool of one upstream server, including ones it adds later | `<endpoint>#server=github` | `Mcp<Name><tag>Session` |
| **Named tools** — only the listed tools of that server | `<endpoint>#server=github&tool=github_a&tool=github_b` | `Mcp<Name><tag>Session` |

`<tag>` is four hex characters derived from the resource URL. It matters most here: two grants
pinning different tools of one upstream server share both the name and the endpoint, so the scope is
the only thing that distinguishes them.

The session API — a typed method per described tool, plus `callTool`, `getActionResult`, and
`listTools` with progressive search/name options — is the same as
[`gatekeeper-mcp`](../gatekeeper-mcp/README.md#what-it-provides).

A server-wide grant can cover more tools than one catalog describes, so its authority is not limited
to the ones with generated signatures. `listTools({ search })` searches beyond the bounded preview
and returns up to 20 compact matches within the shared 5,000-tool / 4 MiB discovery scan;
`listTools({ name })` loads one exact bounded definition, and `callTool` resolves that name under the
same bound before dispatch. Every path rejects names outside the
binding's scope before loading the catalog or contacting the endpoint. Discovery and read results are
recorded as observations; writes retain the ordinary approval flow.

Scoping to one server also shrinks what the agent reads: only that server's tools are rendered as
signatures, and only as many as the budget describes. Additional tools are discovered on demand
within the explicit scan limits above; exceeding a limit fails rather than pretending a tool is absent.

## Configuration

| Variable | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `MCP_PORTAL_URL` | The portal's MCP endpoint. Unset means the connector hides itself. |
| `MCP_PORTAL_NAME` | Display name in the connector list and every approval prompt. Defaults to `MCP Server Portal (<host>)`. |
| `MCP_PORTAL_AUTH` | `oauth` (default), `none`, or `token`. |
| `MCP_PORTAL_TOKEN` | Secret bearer token, for `MCP_PORTAL_AUTH: "token"`. |

| `MCP_PORTAL_HIDDEN_SERVER_IDS` | Comma-separated upstream server IDs to hide from the configurator and refuse at the grant boundary. |

append `?codemode=off` when its policy is default-on. Enforced Code Mode is unsupported. Do not add

```

[ 🔍 GitHub ]

(•) All tools      Every tool this server offers, including ones it adds later.
( ) Choose tools   Only the tools you tick. Anything else is refused, including tools added later.

Allowed tools · Read-only tools return data straight away. The rest queue for your approval.
[ 🔍 Filter tools... ]
12 of 12 selected                                                                     Clear
☑ List issues                                                                     read-only
☑ Create issue                                                               needs approval
```

1. Every tool is named `{server_id}_{original_name}`, split on the first underscore only, and an

`portal_*` tools are excluded from every grant at every scope. `portal_toggle_servers` and friends

own authority. This is a capability-boundary rule, not a policy preference, and is not configurable.

## Approvals and sharing

Identical to [`gatekeeper-mcp`](../gatekeeper-mcp/README.md#approvals-and-sharing), except for the
trust tier. A portal is an aggregator: `destructiveHint` and `idempotentHint` are written by

`addObserver` refuses everyone, as it does for user-supplied endpoints. Reaching the portal is not
the same as being allowed to see a particular tool result, and the Gadget runs on the owner's
credentials regardless. A sharper check is available here than for a bare endpoint —
`portal_list_servers` is per-user and Access-filtered, so it could confirm a collaborator may reach
the same server — but that is still server-granular, not record-granular. See
[`sharing-policy.ts`](../mcp-shared/src/sharing-policy.ts).

## Notes and current limitations

The limitations in
[`gatekeeper-mcp`](../gatekeeper-mcp/README.md#notes-and-current-limitations) apply here too: no
simulation, no revert, no hooks, no scoping below tool names, and `tools/*` only. SSRF is enforced
the same way, by `global_fetch_strictly_public` rather than by hostname patterns. In addition:

- **One portal per deployment.** `MCP_PORTAL_URL` is a single value; a second portal needs a
  second Worker.
- **Server ids come from tool-name prefixes.** An aggregator that flattens tools without prefixing
  them exposes no upstream seam, so this connector finds no server to scope a grant to and the form
  stays unsubmittable. It is not granted as a whole endpoint — that grant does not exist here. Use
  the **MCP** connector (`gatekeeper-mcp`) for such an endpoint, where endpoint-wide breadth is an
  explicit, reviewable choice.

## Layout

| File | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `src/portal.ts` | Vendor, account DO, user, gatekeeper facet, session, configurator RPC |
| `src/config.ts` | Reading and validating the deployment's portal configuration |
| `src/configurator/` | The grant UI (compiled into `src/generated/`) |

Everything else comes from [`@gadgets/mcp-shared`](../mcp-shared/README.md).

## Build & test

```
pnpm exec vp run -F @gadgets/mcp-portal-gatekeeper build   # build:configurator + tsc
pnpm --filter @gadgets/mcp-portal-gatekeeper test:run    # vitest
```

The Worker is run via the root `pnpm dev-server`, not directly.

36:  * Call it at the point of use, every time. Persisting the answer would leave accounts vetted after
37:  * an administrator withdrew the assertion, until each one reconnected.

40:   return (env.MCP_PORTAL_TRUST_ANNOTATIONS ?? "").toLowerCase() === "true" ? "vetted" : "byo";
41: }

43: /** Whether an upstream server is hidden by deployment configuration. */
44: export function isPortalServerHidden(env: Env, serverId: string): boolean {
45:   if (!serverId) return false;

51: /**
52:  * Refuses deployment-hidden servers at the grant boundary. The configurator filter is presentation,
53:  * not authority: an agent can supply a resource URL directly.
54:  */
55: export function requirePortalServerVisible(env: Env, serverId: string): void {
56:   if (!isPortalServerHidden(env, serverId)) return;
57:   throw new Error(
58:     `The portal server "${serverId}" is available through its native connector instead.`,
59:   );
60: }
61: 
62: /**
63:  * Reads the deployment's portal configuration, or null when it is not configured. A missing or
64:  * unusable `MCP_PORTAL_URL` returns null rather than throwing, so the connector advertises no
65:  * resources and the Workshop hides it.
66:  */
67: export function readPortalConfig(env: Env): PortalConfig | null {
68:   const raw = env.MCP_PORTAL_URL?.trim();
69:   if (!raw) return null;
70: 
71:   let url: URL;
72:   try {
73:     url = new URL(raw);
74:   } catch {
75:     return null;
76:   }
77:   // The same rule `guardedFetch` applies anyway. Enforcing it here means an `http://` typo hides the
78:   // connector rather than failing on the first request, with an error naming a URL the user never
79:   // saw.

82:   }
83:   // URL userinfo is an ambient credential: URL and fetch APIs can copy it into requests, while this
84:   // connector also persists and returns the endpoint to users and configurator frames. Portal auth

86:   // contacting a different endpoint than the administrator configured.
87:   if (url.username || url.password) return null;
88:   url.hash = "";
89: 
90:   const configured = env.MCP_PORTAL_AUTH?.trim().toLowerCase();
91:   const auth: ServerAuthKind =
92:     configured === "none" || configured === "token" ? configured : "oauth";

94:   return {
95:     endpoint: url.toString(),
96:     name: env.MCP_PORTAL_NAME?.trim() || `MCP Server Portal (${url.host})`,
97:     auth,
98:   };
99: }

101: /**
102:  * Refuses a grant that does not name one upstream server.
103:  *
104:  * A portal flattens many systems behind one endpoint, so a scope with no `serverId` is a grant over
105:  * all of them at once -- `scopeAllows` permits every tool that is not portal-native -- and that is
106:  * the one breadth this connector deliberately does not offer.
107:  *
108:  * This is the enforcement, not the configurator. The form refuses to *emit* such a URL, but a
109:  * resource URL is not only ever produced by the form: an agent passes a concrete one to
110:  * `requestConnection`, and any URL under the portal's origin reaches `getGatekeeperClassFor`. A
111:  * rule that lives only in the iframe is a suggestion; the facet is minted here. The assertion
112:  * narrows the scope so callers do not need to repeat the invariant.
113:  */
114: export function requirePortalServerScope(
115:   scope: ToolScope,
116: ): asserts scope is ToolScope & { serverId: string } {
117:   if (scope.serverId === undefined) {
118:     throw new Error(
119:       "A portal grant has to name one of the servers behind the portal. Granting the portal itself " +
120:       "would cover every system connected to it, including ones added later.");

122:   if (!isValidToolName(scope.serverId)) throw new Error("Invalid portal server id.");
123:   for (const name of scope.tools ?? []) {
124:     if (!isValidToolName(name)) throw new Error("Invalid MCP tool name.");
125:     if (isPortalNativeTool(name)) {
126:       throw new Error(`Portal management tool "${name}" cannot be granted.`);
127:     }
128:     if (!isPortalToolGrantable(name, scope.serverId)) {
129:       throw new Error(`Tool "${name}" does not belong to portal server "${scope.serverId}".`);
130:     }
131:   }

134: /** Whether one tool may appear in a grant for this portal server. */
135: export function isPortalToolGrantable(name: string, serverId: string): boolean {
136:   return scopeAllows({ serverId }, name, true);
137: }
138: 
139: /** Which catalog evidence is needed to validate one portal scope. */
140: export function portalCatalogValidationMode(
141:   scope: ToolScope & { serverId: string },
142:   reportedServers: readonly Pick<PortalServer, "id">[],
143: ): "named-tools" | "reported-server" | "server-evidence" {
144:   if ((scope.tools?.length ?? 0) > 0) return "named-tools";
145:   return reportedServers.some(server => server.id === scope.serverId)
146:     ? "reported-server"
147:     : "server-evidence";
148: }
149: 
150: /**
151:  * Renders one upstream server's tools as choices on the grant form.
152:  *
153:  * The bounded summaries carry both display text and the annotations classification is decided from,
154:  * so the picker cannot disagree with runtime policy merely because a full schema did not fit.
155:  */
156: export function toolGrantOptions(args: {
157:   serverId: string;
158:   tools: readonly McpTool[];
159:   trust: ServerTrust;
160: }): ConfiguratorUIOption[] {
161:   return args.tools.map(tool => {
162:     return {
163:       value: tool.name,
164:       // Within a chosen server the `{server_id}_` prefix is noise, so it is shown stripped while
165:       // `value` keeps the wire name the grant is actually recorded with.
166:       title: tool.title ?? tool.name.slice(args.serverId.length + 1),
167:       subtitle: tool.description?.split(/\r?\n/)[0],
168:       // Surfaced here so the person granting can see, per tool, whether calls will interrupt them.
169:       meta: classifyTool(tool, args.trust).mode === "read"
170:         ? "read-only"
171:         : "needs approval",
172:     };
173:   });
174: }
175: 
176: /** The single resource type this connector offers, scoped to the configured portal's origin. */
177: export function portalResource(config: PortalConfig): SupportedResource {
178:   return {
179:     // Origin-scoped, so a resource URL for anything else matches nothing this connector offers.
180:     urlPattern: `${new URL(config.endpoint).origin}/*`,
181:     title: config.name,
182:     description:
183:       "Tools from the servers behind this portal. Writes need approval.",
184:   };
185: }
186: 
187: /**
188:  * The connected-server record stored on an account, derived entirely from configuration.
189:  * `provenance` is what keeps the far side from renaming itself over `MCP_PORTAL_NAME` in every
190:  * approval prompt (see `McpAccountBase.complete`).
191:  */
192: export function portalServer(config: PortalConfig): ConnectedServer {
193:   return {
194:     endpoint: config.endpoint,
195:     provenance: "deployment",
196:     auth: config.auth,
197:     serverId: PORTAL_SERVER_ID,
198:     serverName: config.name,
199:   };
200: }
201: 
202: /**
203:  * Probing may legitimately move between none and OAuth. A preissued token is deployment authority,
204:  * so entering or leaving that mode requires the account to reconnect against current configuration.
205:  */
206: export function portalAuthRequiresReconnect(
207:   connected: ServerAuthKind, configured: ServerAuthKind,
208: ): boolean {
209:   return (connected === "token") !== (configured === "token");
210: }
211: 
212: /**
213:  * The preissued token, but only for the endpoint the deployment currently names.
214:  *
215:  * `MCP_PORTAL_TOKEN` is the one credential in this connector read from live configuration rather
216:  * than from an account's storage. Everything else an account hands out was minted for the endpoint
217:  * that account records, so it is safe to send there by construction. This is not: an administrator
218:  * repoints the gateway by editing the URL and its token together, which touches no account, so
219:  * until someone reconnects the account still names the old host while this value is already the new
220:  * deployment's secret. An account-side endpoint check cannot catch that -- it compares the caller
221:  * against storage that has not moved yet -- so the scoping has to happen here, against the
222:  * configuration the token actually belongs to.
223:  *
224:  * Null means "this deployment has no token for that endpoint", covering both a portal with no token
225:  * configured and one that has since been repointed. Callers fail the request closed either way.
226:  */
227: export function portalTokenFor(env: Env, endpoint: string): string | null {
228:   const config = readPortalConfig(env);
229:   if (config?.auth !== "token" || !sameEndpoint(config.endpoint, endpoint)) return null;
230:   return env.MCP_PORTAL_TOKEN || null;
231: }

154:  * name. A reported server needs no catalog scan; an unreported server needs one prefixed tool as

158:   env: Env,

368:    * The portal as currently configured, not as it was when this account connected. Repointing the
369:    * deployment therefore surfaces as a reconnect, via `getGatekeeperClassFor` refusing the old
370:    * endpoint, rather than as a Gadget quietly talking to a portal nobody chose.
371:    */
372:   async getSupportedResources(): Promise<SupportedResource[]> {
373:     const config = readPortalConfig(this.env);
374:     return config ? [portalResource(config)] : [];
375:   }
376: 
377:   async getGatekeeperClassFor(url: string): Promise<{
378:     class: DurableObjectClass<Gatekeeper<unknown>>;
379:     resource: SupportedResource;
380:   }> {
381:     const config = readPortalConfig(this.env);
382:     if (!config) {
383:       throw new Error("This deployment has no MCP server portal configured.");
384:     }
385:     const server = await this.#account().getServer();
386:     const resource = portalResource(config);
387: 
388:     // The account connected to one portal and the deployment now names one; a repoint between the
389:     // two must surface as a reconnect. Otherwise this facet would be minted against the endpoint
390:     // frozen on the account while the deployment believes it configured a different one.
391:     if (!sameEndpoint(server.endpoint, config.endpoint)) {
392:       throw new Error(
393:         `This connection is for ${hostOf(server.endpoint)}, but this deployment's portal is now ` +
394:         `${hostOf(config.endpoint)}. Reconnect the account.`);
395:     }
396:     if (portalAuthRequiresReconnect(server.auth, config.auth)) {
397:       throw new Error("This deployment's portal authentication changed. Reconnect the account.");
398:     }
399: 
400:     // The account holds credentials for one portal, so a resource URL naming any other endpoint is
401:     // not this account's to grant. Compared in full rather than by origin: one host can front `/mcp`
402:     // and `/mcp-v2` as unrelated endpoints, and the facet always calls the endpoint recorded on the
403:     // account, so an origin-only test would honour a grant against a URL nobody connected to.
404:     const requested = new URL(url, server.endpoint);
405:     if (!sameEndpoint(requested.toString(), config.endpoint)) {
406:       throw new Error(
407:         `This connection is for ${config.endpoint}, not ` +
408:         `${endpointOfResourceUrl(requested)}.`);
409:     }
410:     if (!matchesResourceUrlPattern(resource.urlPattern, requested.toString())) {
411:       throw new Error(`"${url}" does not match this connection's resource type.`);
412:     }
413: 
414:     const account = this.#account();
415:     const { scope, upstream } = await validatePortalScope(
416:       this.env, account, server.endpoint, requested);
417: 
418:     const props: McpGatekeeperImplProps = {
419:       accountObjectId: this.ctx.props.accountObjectId,
420:       endpoint: server.endpoint,
421:       serverId: server.serverId,
422:       serverName: config.name,
423:       scopeServerName: upstream?.name ?? scope.serverId,
424:       scope,
425:     };
426:     return { class: this.ctx.exports.McpGatekeeperImpl({ props }), resource };
427:   }
428: 
429:   async startResourceConfigurator(_resourceUrlPattern: string): Promise<ResourceConfiguratorFrame> {
430:     return {
431:       iframeHtml: MCP_SERVER_CONFIGURATOR_HTML,
432:       ui: new RpcStub(new McpServerConfiguratorUI(this.env, this.#account())),
433:     };
434:   }
435: 
436:   @skipRpcValidation()
437:   async getVerifier(): Promise<Fetcher<GatekeeperUserVerifier>> {
438:     return this.ctx.exports.McpPortalVerifier({});
439:   }
440: }
441: 
442: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
443: // Verifier
444: 
445: // Required by the `GatekeeperUser` contract but never interrogated, since `addObserver` refuses
446: // everyone.
447: @validateRpc()
448: export class McpPortalVerifier
449:   extends WorkerEntrypoint<Env>
450:   implements GatekeeperUserVerifier
451: {
452:   verify(): void {}
453: }
454: 
455: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
456: // Resource configurator
457: 
458: @validateRpc()
459: class McpServerConfiguratorUI extends RpcTarget implements McpServerConfiguratorRpc {
460:   #env: Env;
461:   #account: DurableObjectStub<McpAccount>;
462:   #serverPromise: Promise<ConnectedServer> | undefined;
463:   #portalServersPromise: Promise<PortalServer[]> | undefined;
464: 
465:   constructor(env: Env, account: DurableObjectStub<McpAccount>) {
466:     super();
467:     this.#env = env;
468:     this.#account = account;
469:   }
470: 
471:   async getEndpoint(): Promise<string> {
472:     return (await this.#server()).endpoint;
473:   }
474: 
475:   #server(): Promise<ConnectedServer> {
476:     return this.#serverPromise ??= this.#account.getServer();
477:   }
478: 
479:   #portalServers(): Promise<PortalServer[]> {
480:     return this.#portalServersPromise ??= (async () => {
481:       const server = await this.#server();
482:       return listAvailablePortalServers(this.#env, this.#account, server.endpoint);
483:     })();
484:   }
485: 
486:   // Ask the portal for its server index without first loading every upstream tool. Empty for an
487:   // endpoint that does not implement the portal contract or currently fronts nothing; either case
488:   // leaves the form unsubmittable.
489:   async listServerOptions(): Promise<ConfiguratorUIOption[]> {
490:     return (await this.#portalServers())
491:       .filter(upstream => !isPortalServerHidden(this.#env, upstream.id))
492:       .map(upstream => ({
493:         value: upstream.id,
494:         title: upstream.name,
495:         // A server can be configured but switched off for this session, making a grant onto it valid
496:         // but presently empty, which the person choosing should see.
497:         meta: upstream.enabled ? undefined : "disabled in portal",
498:       }));
499:   }
500: 
501:   // Tools the grant may cover within one portal upstream server. The survey is checked before the
502:   // detailed catalog is fetched, and `toolGrantOptions` decides what each source says.
503:   async listToolOptions(serverId: string): Promise<ConfiguratorUIOption[]> {
504:     if (!isValidToolName(serverId) || isPortalServerHidden(this.#env, serverId)) return [];
505:     if (!(await this.#portalServers()).some(server => server.id === serverId)) return [];
506:     const server = await this.#server();
507:     const tools = await withClient(this.#env, this.#account, server.endpoint,
508:       client => client.listMatchingToolSummaries(
509:         MAX_TOOLS_PER_SERVER,
510:         tool => isPortalToolGrantable(tool.name, serverId),
511:       ));
512:     return toolGrantOptions({
513:       serverId,
514:       tools,
515:       trust: portalTrust(this.#env),
516:     });
517:   }
518: }
519: 
520: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
521: // Gatekeeper facet
522: 
523: // Props identifying which server (and how much of it) a gatekeeper facet governs. The trust tier is
524: // absent: it is deployment configuration, read from `portalTrust(this.env)` at each point of use,
525: // since baking it into props would pin every binding to the setting on the day it was created.
526: type McpGatekeeperImplProps = {
527:   accountObjectId: string;
528:   endpoint: string;
529:   serverId: string;
530:   serverName: string;
531:   // Optional for facets minted before catalog-backed validation persisted the upstream display name.
532:   scopeServerName?: string;
533:   // How much of one upstream server this binding may call.
534:   scope: ToolScope & { serverId: string };
535: };
536: 
537: export class McpGatekeeperImpl
538:   extends McpFacetBase<Env, McpGatekeeperImplProps, McpSessionImpl> {
539: 
540:   protected get log() {
541:     return logger.with({
542:       serverId: this.ctx.props.serverId,
543:       serverHost: hostOf(this.ctx.props.endpoint),

548:   protected account(): ConnectionAccount {

550:       this.ctx.exports.McpAccount.idFromString(this.ctx.props.accountObjectId));
551:   }
552: 
553:   protected get trust(): ServerTrust {

555:   }
556: 
557:   protected get sessionClass() {
558:     return McpSessionImpl;
559:   }
560: 
561:   protected get observerName(): string {
562:     return this.#scopeLabel();
563:   }
564: 
565:   // How this binding's breadth reads to a human, for approval prompts and the bindings list.
566:   #scopeLabel(): string {
567:     const { scope, serverName, scopeServerName } = this.ctx.props;
568:     return `${serverName} / ${scopeServerName ?? scope.serverId}`;
569:   }
570: 
571:   async describe(): Promise<ResourceDescription> {
572:     const tools = await this.tools();
573:     const reads = tools.filter(entry => entry.mode === "read").length;
574:     const { scope } = this.ctx.props;
575:     const label = this.#scopeLabel();
576: 
577:     const counts = `${reads} read-only, ${tools.length - reads} requiring approval`;
578:     const plural = tools.length === 1 ? "" : "s";
579:     const snippet = scope.tools
580:       ? `${scope.tools.length} named MCP tool${scope.tools.length === 1 ? "" : "s"} on ` +
581:         `${label} \u2014 ${counts}. Other tools are refused.`
582:       : `All tools of the ${this.ctx.props.scopeServerName ?? scope.serverId} server on ` +
583:         `${this.ctx.props.serverName}; ${tools.length} tool definition${plural} shown here ` +
584:         `(${counts}). Use listTools({ search }) for others. Other servers are refused.`;
585: 
586:     return {
587:       url: this.resourceUrl,
588:       title: scope.tools?.length === 1 ? `${label}: ${scope.tools[0]}` : label,
589:       snippet,
590:       suggestedBindingName: `MCP_${bindingNameFragment(this.#bindingId())}`,
591:       tsType: sessionTypeName(this.#bindingId(), this.resourceUrl),
592:     };
593:   }
594: 
595:   // Identifies this binding's shape for naming. Server-scoped bindings get their own suggested name
596:   // and session type, so two bindings onto different servers of one portal do not collide and the
597:   // agent's type for the GitHub half of a portal is named after GitHub.
598:   //
599:   // This is a readable label, not an identity: two grants pinning different tools of one upstream
600:   // server produce the same id. `sessionTypeName` is what separates them, from the scoped resource
601:   // URL.
602:   #bindingId(): string {

604:     return `${serverId}-${scope.serverId}`;
605:   }

607:   /**
608:    * Namespaces persistent approval policy by both the readable binding shape and the exact portal
609:    * endpoint. A deployment repoint must not carry an always-approve decision to a different system
610:    * merely because both portals expose a tool with the same name.
611:    */
612:   protected get actionScopeTag(): string {

614:   }

616:   async getTypeScriptTypes(): Promise<string> {

622:       discriminator: this.resourceUrl,
623:       trust: portalTrust(this.env),
624:       tools: await this.tools(),

628:   /**

2: // unnamed agent capsule (ContextGatekeeper) and a management UI (ContextApi). Data is sharing-domain

9:   VendorDescription, AccountDescription, AgentCatalog,

11:   GatekeeperConnectCallback, GatekeeperConnectOptions, SupportedResource,
12:   Gatekeeper, GatekeeperUserVerifier, ResourceDescription, ActionKind,

1: // Agent read path over enabled collections. Every returned result is authorized as an observation
2: // and attributed to the collections whose metadata or content it reveals.
3: 
4: import { RpcStub as NativeRpcStub } from "cloudflare:workers";
5: import { RpcTarget } from "capnweb";
6: import { validateRpc } from "capnweb-validate";
7: import type {
8:   ObservationAuthorizer, ObservationDescription,
9: } from "@gadgets/workshop-shared/gatekeeper";
10: import {
11:   ContextSearchResult, ContextListing, ContextListingEntry, ContextReadResult,
12:   ContextCollectionVisibility, decodeDocId, encodeDocId, isTextContentType, VENDOR_ID,
13: } from "./context-types.js";
14: import type { ContextCollectionDurableObject } from "./context-collection.js";
15: import type { UserLibraryDurableObject } from "./user-library.js";
16: import { domainName } from "./domain.js";
17: import { obsContext } from "./observability.js";
18: 
19: const logger = obsContext.createLogger({
20:   component: "gatekeeper.context", vendorId: VENDOR_ID,
21: });
22: 
23: // Fanout cap for whole-library search/list.
24: const MAX_COLLECTION_FANOUT = 8;
25: 
26: type ObserveCollections = (collectionIds: string[]) => Promise<{
27:   excludeObservers?: string[];
28:   pendingCollections: string[];
29:   commit(): void;
30: }>;
31: 
32: @validateRpc()
33: export class LibraryReadSession extends RpcTarget {
34:   // Per-session enabled set. Visibility is retained by the source API, though observer enforcement
35:   // uses collection-level access checks rather than the old sticky sharing prohibition.
36:   #enabledPromise?: Promise<Map<string, ContextCollectionVisibility>>;
37: 
38:   constructor(
39:     private collections: DurableObjectNamespace<ContextCollectionDurableObject>,
40:     private userLibraries: DurableObjectNamespace<UserLibraryDurableObject>,
41:     private domain: string,
42:     private accountId: string,
43:     private authorizer: NativeRpcStub<ObservationAuthorizer>,
44:     private observeCollections: ObserveCollections,
45:   ) {
46:     super();
47:   }
48: 
49:   /** Release the authorizer owned by this read session. */
50:   [Symbol.dispose](): void {
51:     this.authorizer[Symbol.dispose]?.();
52:   }
53: 
54:   #collection(id: string): DurableObjectStub<ContextCollectionDurableObject> {
55:     return this.collections.get(this.collections.idFromName(domainName(this.domain, id)));
56:   }
57: 
58:   #userLib(): DurableObjectStub<UserLibraryDurableObject> {
59:     return this.userLibraries.get(this.userLibraries.idFromName(domainName(this.domain, this.accountId)));
60:   }
61: 
62:   // Computed once per session; search/list/read share it.
63:   #enabled(): Promise<Map<string, ContextCollectionVisibility>> {
64:     return (this.#enabledPromise ??= this.#userLib().getEnabledCollections(this.domain));
65:   }
66: 
67:   async #authorize(
68:       collectionIds: string[], description: ObservationDescription): Promise<void> {
69:     let check = collectionIds.length > 0
70:       ? await this.observeCollections(collectionIds)
71:       : { pendingCollections: [], commit() {} };
72:     await this.authorizer.authorizeObservation({
73:       ...description, excludeObservers: check.excludeObservers,
74:     });
75:     check.commit();
76:   }
77: 
78:   async search(query: string, opts?: {
79:     collectionId?: string;
80:     limit?: number;
81:   }): Promise<ContextSearchResult[]> {
82:     let enabled = await this.#enabled();
83:     let limit = opts?.limit ?? 20;
84: 
85:     let targetIds: string[];
86:     if (opts?.collectionId) {
87:       if (!enabled.has(opts.collectionId)) return [];
88:       targetIds = [opts.collectionId];
89:     } else {
90:       targetIds = [...enabled.keys()];
91:     }
92: 
93:     let perCollection = await mapWithConcurrency(targetIds, MAX_COLLECTION_FANOUT, async (collectionId) => {
94:       try {
95:         let hits = await this.#collection(collectionId).search(query, limit);
96:         return hits.map((r): ContextSearchResult => ({
97:           docId: encodeDocId(collectionId, r.path),
98:           collectionId,
99:           title: r.name,
100:           path: r.path,
101:           description: r.description,
102:           snippet: r.snippet,
103:           score: r.score,
104:         }));
105:       } catch (err) {
106:         logger.warn("failed to search collection", {
107:           event: "collection.search.failed", collectionId, error: err,
108:         });
109:         return [];
110:       }
111:     });
112: 
113:     let results = perCollection.flat();
114:     results.sort((a, b) => (b.score ?? 0) - (a.score ?? 0));
115:     results = results.slice(0, limit);
116: 
117:     // Nothing matched → nothing was observed, so don't record an observation (mirrors read()).
118:     if (results.length === 0) return results;
119:     let collectionIds = [...new Set(results.map(r => r.collectionId).filter((id): id is string => !!id))];
120:     // Authorize after fetching, before returning data.
121:     await this.#authorize(collectionIds, {
122:       title: `Context search: ${query}`,
123:       description:
124:         `Searched the Context Library for \`${query}\`. Returned ${results.length} result(s)` +
125:         (collectionIds.length ? ` across ${collectionIds.length} collection(s).` : "."),
126:     });
127:     return results;
128:   }

131:     collectionId?: string;
132:     path?: string;
133:   }): Promise<ContextListing> {
134:     let listing = await this.#fetchListing(opts);

136:     if (listing.entries.length === 0) return listing;
137:     // Both collection contents and top-level collection titles/descriptions reveal collection data.
138:     let collectionIds = opts?.collectionId

161:     let enabled = await this.#enabled();

164:     let doc = await this.#collection(collectionId).getContextDocument(path);
165:     // No document found (missing or inaccessible) → nothing was observed, so don't record one.
166:     if (!doc) return null;
167: 
168:     await this.#authorize([collectionId], {
169:       title: `Context read: ${doc.name}`,
170:       description: `Read Context Library document \`${docId}\`.`,
171:     });

174:       ? doc.body
175:       : `data:${doc.contentType};base64,${doc.body}`;
176:     return {
177:       docId,
178:       title: doc.name,
179:       path: doc.path,
180:       description: doc.description,
181:       content,
182:     };
183:   }
184: 
185:   // Fetch without recording; list() authorizes.
186:   async #fetchListing(opts?: { collectionId?: string; path?: string }): Promise<ContextListing> {
187:     let enabled = await this.#enabled();
188: 
189:     if (!opts?.collectionId) {
190:       let collectionEntries = await mapWithConcurrency([...enabled.keys()], MAX_COLLECTION_FANOUT,
191:         async (collectionId): Promise<ContextListingEntry | null> => {
192:           try {
193:             let meta = await this.#collection(collectionId).getMetadata();
194:             return {
195:               type: "collection",
196:               id: collectionId,
197:               title: meta.title,
198:               description: meta.description,

248:   let results: R[] = Array.from({ length: items.length });
249:   let next = 0;

251:     while (next < items.length) {
252:       let i = next++;

254:     }
255:   }

1: # Scheduled Tasks
2: 
3: Scheduled Tasks is an ambient Gatekeeper that lets workspace code register persistent callbacks for
4: elapsed intervals, wall-clock recurrences, and one-time runs. Each account also gets a read-only
5: management app at `/gatekeepers/scheduler`.
6: 
7: ## User flow
8: 
9: 1. Ask the agent to create a scheduled task, or open **Scheduled** and choose a starter prompt.
10: 2. Confirm what the task should do, the workspace and resources it may use, its cadence, and its
11:    IANA timezone when it uses wall-clock time.
12: 3. The agent registers a persistent callback. Registration creates a disabled hook and returns its
13:    schedule ID; it does not start the schedule.
14: 4. Enable the hook in the Workshop's Connections UI.
15: 5. Use **Scheduled** to search and inspect schedules across the account. Select a schedule row to
16:    open its workspace.
17: 
18: The Scheduler app is intentionally read-only. Enabling and disabling remain in Connections; the app
19: does not provide editing, pausing, deletion, run history, or a second hook toggle.
20: 
21: ## Agent API
22: 
23: The ambient binding exposes `ScheduleSession`. The exact agent-facing contract and examples live in
24: [`src/types.d.ts`](src/types.d.ts).
25: 
26: ```ts
27: const callback = await ctx.restore({ type: "dailyBrief" });
28: 
29: const scheduleId = await SCHEDULER.calendarAt(
30:   {
31:     timeZone: "America/Chicago",
32:     freq: "weekly",
33:     byDay: ["MO", "TU", "WE", "TH", "FR"],
34:     hour: 8,
35:     minute: 0,
36:   },
37:   callback,
38:   {
39:     title: "Daily brief",
40:     description: "Prepare the morning calendar and inbox brief.",
41:     occurrences: { count: 10 },
42:   },
43: );
44: ```
45: 
46: Use the three registration methods according to the user's intent:
47: 
48: - `every(everyMs, callback, options)` uses elapsed UTC time. The minimum interval is 60 seconds.
49: - `calendarAt(rule, callback, options)` follows local wall-clock time and requires an explicit IANA
50:   timezone. It supports hourly, daily, and weekly rules.
51: - `runAt(when, callback, options)` runs once at an absolute epoch-millisecond timestamp or an
52:   explicit timezone-aware wall-clock time.
53: 
54: Recurring `every()` and `calendarAt()` calls may stop after a finite bound. Give one or the other,
55: never both; `runAt()` accepts neither.
56: 
57: - `occurrences: { count: 10 }` allows ten logical scheduled occurrences.
58: - `occurrences: { until: { timeZone, year, month, day, hour, minute } }` allows occurrences through
59:   that instant, inclusively. An absolute epoch-millisecond `until` is also accepted. Registration
60:   rejects a cutoff that precedes the schedule's first occurrence.
61: 
62: The count bounds *due slots*, not successful runs. A slot consumes one count as soon as it becomes
63: due and takes a `runId`, even if admission or callback delivery then fails; admission failures skip
64: the slot without retrying it. Retries reuse the same `runId` and do not consume another count.
65: Missed occurrences remain skipped and do not count.
66: 
67: A bound is checked against live state, so a schedule that reaches it reports `completed`. A schedule
68: whose cutoff already passed by the time its hook is enabled reports `expired` instead: it never got
69: a slot. A schedule whose callback exhausts its eight attempts reports `dead` and stops there,
70: whether or not the bound was reached — a `count: 10` schedule that dies on its third occurrence
71: never reaches the fourth. Disabling a hook drops its driver state, so re-enabling the same schedule
72: restarts the count — treat `count` as a bound per enablement, not a lifetime guarantee.
73: 
74: `list()` returns active and terminal schedules for enabled hooks in the current workspace only. It
75: does not expose schedules from other workspaces in the account.
76: 
77: ## Persistent callbacks and retries
78: 
79: Callbacks implement `ScheduledTaskHook.onSchedule()` and must be made persistent with
80: `ctx.restore()` before registration. Each firing contains:
81: 
82: - `scheduleId`, the stable registration ID;
83: - `runId`, stable across retries of one logical occurrence;
84: - `scheduledTime`, the planned Unix epoch time;
85: - `actualTime`, the current delivery-attempt time; and
86: - `timeZone`, the schedule's display timezone (`UTC` for elapsed intervals and numeric one-shots).
87: 
88: Callback delivery is best-effort within a bounded retry window and may occur more than once. Callback
89: code should use `runId` as an idempotency key. Authorization or callback failures retry up to eight
90: total attempts with exponential delays beginning at one minute and capped at one hour. Exhausted
91: schedules enter the **Needs attention** state.
92: 
93: The Workshop admission check runs before every attempt. If the hook, gatekeeper, or account is no
94: longer allowed, the occurrence is skipped without consuming a callback attempt. Recurring schedules
95: advance to their next future occurrence; a due one-shot expires.
96: 
97: ## Cadence behavior
98: 
99: - Recurrences preserve the phase established at registration.
100: - Missed occurrences are skipped, not replayed or caught up.
101: - Fixed intervals measure elapsed time and therefore shift relative to local clocks across DST.
102: - Calendar schedules retain their requested local wall-clock cadence across DST.
103: - A nonexistent spring-forward time moves forward by the transition gap.
104: - An ambiguous fall-back time uses the earlier instant and fires once.
105: - Date-less wall-clock one-shots resolve to the next future occurrence of that local time.
106: 
107: Always ask the user for the timezone of a wall-clock schedule. Do not infer it from locale or silently
108: choose UTC.
109: 
110: ## Lifecycle
111: 
112: Registration only binds a disabled Workshop hook; it writes no schedule row. Enabling records the
113: target workspace ID and optional gadget ID, then creates the account-driver row and arms its alarm.
114: Disabling removes the row and its stored capabilities. Re-enabling creates fresh active state,
115: preserves the original recurrence phase, and does not replay missed work. A repeated enable while
116: the row still exists instead preserves its current schedule state and refreshes its activation details.

2. Confirm what the task should do, the workspace and resources it may use, its cadence, and its

display.text:
# Scheduled Tasks

Scheduled Tasks is an ambient Gatekeeper that lets workspace code register persistent callbacks for
elapsed intervals, wall-clock recurrences, and one-time runs. Each account also gets a read-only
management app at `/gatekeepers/scheduler`.

## User flow

1. Ask the agent to create a scheduled task, or open **Scheduled** and choose a starter prompt.
2. Confirm what the task should do, the workspace and resources it may use, its cadence, and its
   IANA timezone when it uses wall-clock time.
3. The agent registers a persistent callback. Registration creates a disabled hook and returns its
   schedule ID; it does not start the schedule.
4. Enable the hook in the Workshop's Connections UI.
5. Use **Scheduled** to search and inspect schedules across the account. Select a schedule row to
   open its workspace.

The Scheduler app is intentionally read-only. Enabling and disabling remain in Connections; the app
does not provide editing, pausing, deletion, run history, or a second hook toggle.

## Agent API

The ambient binding exposes `ScheduleSession`. The exact agent-facing contract and examples live in
[`src/types.d.ts`](src/types.d.ts).

```ts
const callback = await ctx.restore({ type: "dailyBrief" });

const scheduleId = await SCHEDULER.calendarAt(
  {
    timeZone: "America/Chicago",
    freq: "weekly",
    byDay: ["MO", "TU", "WE", "TH", "FR"],
    hour: 8,
    minute: 0,
  },
  callback,
  {
    title: "Daily brief",
    description: "Prepare the morning calendar and inbox brief.",
    occurrences: { count: 10 },
  },
);
```

Use the three registration methods according to the user's intent:

- `every(everyMs, callback, options)` uses elapsed UTC time. The minimum interval is 60 seconds.
- `calendarAt(rule, callback, options)` follows local wall-clock time and requires an explicit IANA
  timezone. It supports hourly, daily, and weekly rules.
- `runAt(when, callback, options)` runs once at an absolute epoch-millisecond timestamp or an
  explicit timezone-aware wall-clock time.

Recurring `every()` and `calendarAt()` calls may stop after a finite bound. Give one or the other,
never both; `runAt()` accepts neither.

- `occurrences: { count: 10 }` allows ten logical scheduled occurrences.
- `occurrences: { until: { timeZone, year, month, day, hour, minute } }` allows occurrences through
  that instant, inclusively. An absolute epoch-millisecond `until` is also accepted. Registration
  rejects a cutoff that precedes the schedule's first occurrence.

The count bounds *due slots*, not successful runs. A slot consumes one count as soon as it becomes
due and takes a `runId`, even if admission or callback delivery then fails; admission failures skip
the slot without retrying it. Retries reuse the same `runId` and do not consume another count.
Missed occurrences remain skipped and do not count.

A bound is checked against live state, so a schedule that reaches it reports `completed`. A schedule
whose cutoff already passed by the time its hook is enabled reports `expired` instead: it never got
a slot. A schedule whose callback exhausts its eight attempts reports `dead` and stops there,
whether or not the bound was reached — a `count: 10` schedule that dies on its third occurrence
never reaches the fourth. Disabling a hook drops its driver state, so re-enabling the same schedule
restarts the count — treat `count` as a bound per enablement, not a lifetime guarantee.

`list()` returns active and terminal schedules for enabled hooks in the current workspace only. It
does not expose schedules from other workspaces in the account.

## Persistent callbacks and retries

Callbacks implement `ScheduledTaskHook.onSchedule()` and must be made persistent with
`ctx.restore()` before registration. Each firing contains:

- `scheduleId`, the stable registration ID;
- `runId`, stable across retries of one logical occurrence;
- `scheduledTime`, the planned Unix epoch time;
- `actualTime`, the current delivery-attempt time; and
- `timeZone`, the schedule's display timezone (`UTC` for elapsed intervals and numeric one-shots).

Callback delivery is best-effort within a bounded retry window and may occur more than once. Callback
code should use `runId` as an idempotency key. Authorization or callback failures retry up to eight
total attempts with exponential delays beginning at one minute and capped at one hour. Exhausted
schedules enter the **Needs attention** state.

The Workshop admission check runs before every attempt. If the hook, gatekeeper, or account is no
longer allowed, the occurrence is skipped without consuming a callback attempt. Recurring schedules
advance to their next future occurrence; a due one-shot expires.

## Cadence behavior

- Recurrences preserve the phase established at registration.
- Missed occurrences are skipped, not replayed or caught up.
- Fixed intervals measure elapsed time and therefore shift relative to local clocks across DST.
- Calendar schedules retain their requested local wall-clock cadence across DST.
- A nonexistent spring-forward time moves forward by the transition gap.
- An ambiguous fall-back time uses the earlier instant and fires once.
- Date-less wall-clock one-shots resolve to the next future occurrence of that local time.

Always ask the user for the timezone of a wall-clock schedule. Do not infer it from locale or silently
choose UTC.

## Lifecycle

Registration only binds a disabled Workshop hook; it writes no schedule row. Enabling records the
target workspace ID and optional gadget ID, then creates the account-driver row and arms its alarm.
Disabling removes the row and its stored capabilities. Re-enabling creates fresh active state,
preserves the original recurrence phase, and does not replay missed work. A repeated enable while
the row still exists instead preserves its current schedule state and refreshes its activation details.

Successful one-shots become **Finished**. Past or rejected one-shots become expired. Terminal rows
remain visible and consume enabled-schedule quota until their hook is disabled in Connections.
Creating a workspace from a blueprint does not copy schedules or capabilities: the new workspace must
register its callback and receive fresh enablement.

Disconnecting the Scheduler account revokes its driver, deletes schedule state, and leaves a permanent
tombstone so retained stale controllers cannot recreate the account.

## Management app

The account advertises its UI through the generic `AccountDescription.providesUi` mechanism, the same
mechanism used by other Gatekeeper management apps. The Workshop discovers it dynamically and hosts
the single-file app in an opaque-origin, network-isolated `srcDoc` frame.

The app can only call its account-scoped, read-only `list()` capability plus bounded host methods for
theme updates, workspace-title resolution, navigation, and starter prompts. Pages contain at most 100
schedules. Search is case-insensitive over title and description and is limited to 200 characters.
Cursors are opaque, bounded, and tied to the normalized search and status filters.

The **All**, **Active**, **Needs attention**, and **Finished** tabs map to the projected
`active`, `dead`, and `completed`/`expired` statuses. Target metadata is presentation data only;
opening its validated internal route grants no new authority. Create and starter actions place fixed
editable text in the Home composer and never submit it automatically.

## Architecture and security

Each Scheduler account owns one SQLite-backed `ScheduleDriver` Durable Object and one alarm for all of
its workspaces. Workspace sessions inherit their opaque scope from the containing Overseer facet;
callers cannot supply an account or workspace ID. Plain schedule metadata and reconstructable RPC
capabilities are stored under separate keys and changed transactionally.

The alarm persists state before crossing an RPC boundary. It processes at most 20 due schedules per
pass with four concurrent deliveries, then arms an immediate continuation when a backlog remains.
Stable `runId` fencing prevents late completion or retry continuations from mutating a disabled,
re-enabled, or revoked schedule.

One account-wide driver keeps management and revocation simple, but it is also a shared failure domain:
a user callback that never settles can delay other schedules in that account until the runtime aborts
the alarm. Bounded batches limit ordinary load; they do not eliminate that tradeoff.

The Scheduler is capability-authorized. It does not receive Workshop user identity, assert its own
ambient policy, expose external network authority, or implement actions. The Workshop's existing hook
admission and observation authorization remain the security boundaries.

## Limits

- 500 enabled or terminal schedule rows per account.
- 100 enabled or terminal schedule rows per workspace.
- 100 rows per management page.
- 20 due schedules per alarm pass and four concurrent deliveries.
- Eight callback attempts per logical occurrence.
- Schedule titles: 200 characters; descriptions: 2,000 characters.

These are fixed policy limits rather than deployment settings.

## Development

Install and build from the repository root:

```sh
pnpm install
pnpm --filter @gadgets/gatekeeper-scheduler test:run
pnpm --filter @gadgets/gatekeeper-scheduler build
pnpm run dev-server
pnpm run dev-client
```

The development server discovers `gatekeeper-*` packages, builds `app/` into the generated single-file
asset, and creates the local `GATEKEEPER_SCHEDULER` service binding. Do not edit generated local
Wrangler configuration.

Worker code gets its runtime and `Cloudflare.Env` types from generated
[`worker-configuration.d.ts`](worker-configuration.d.ts), referenced by `tsconfig.json`. Regenerate it
with Wrangler after changing Worker configuration; do not hand-maintain a parallel `Env` interface.
The browser app uses the separate DOM-only `tsconfig.app.json` and imports only environment-neutral
management DTOs.

## Deployment

Before exposing Scheduler:

1. Deploy the Workshop hook target-metadata contract and the `startHook()` admission backstop.
2. Deploy this Worker so its `ScheduleDriver` and `SchedulerGatekeeper` SQLite migration exists.
3. Add `GATEKEEPER_SCHEDULER` to the deployment's Workshop service bindings.

Scheduler declares only that it can auto-provision an account. Workshop provisioning policy defaults
the `scheduler` vendor to **optional**; an administrator can explicitly choose disabled, optional, or
enabled. Production service bindings are site-specific and are not generated by this package.

The `allow_irrevocable_stub_storage` compatibility flag is required while stored callback capabilities
exist and must not be removed from an existing deployment.

## Troubleshooting

- **Scheduled is missing from navigation:** confirm the Scheduler binding exists, the vendor is enabled
  or optional with a connected account, and account discovery returns `providesUi`.
- **A new schedule is not listed or running:** registration starts disabled. Enable its hook in the
  workspace Connections UI.
- **A schedule says Needs attention:** callback authorization or execution exhausted its retry budget.
  Fix the callback or resource access, then disable and re-enable the hook.
- **A one-shot says Expired:** its firing time passed without admission or it was already past when
  enabled. Register a new future one-shot.
- **A recurrence appears an hour off:** use `calendarAt()` for local wall-clock intent and `every()` for
  elapsed time; verify the explicit IANA timezone.
- **A blueprint-created workspace has no schedules:** schedules are deliberately not copied. Register
  them again in the new workspace.

## Non-goals

V1 does not provide schedule editing, local pause/toggle/delete controls, recurring run history,
`lastRunAt`, account default timezones, actor attribution, blueprint schedule cloning, catch-up delivery,
or collaborator-owned schedule routing. Hook lifecycle remains in the Workshop Connections UI.
