1: # Gatekeeper Cloudflare
2: 
3: This package provides Cloudflare OAuth integration for Gadgets. It serves three purposes:
4: 
5: - **Sign-in:** when `cloudflare` is in the deployment's `AUTH_GATEKEEPERS` allowlist, "Continue with
6:   Cloudflare" appears on the login page. The grant reads the account email (verified by Cloudflare,
7:   via the `/user` API), which becomes the user's identity. Cloudflare sign-in also establishes the
8:   persistent billing-only connection described below.
9: - **AI Gateway billing:** when a user connects Cloudflare or signs in with it, the billing scopes are
10:   requested and the connection persists. The Workshop then reads a usable access
11:   token from it (`getUsableAccessToken`) to power the [AI Gateway billing](../../docs/ai-gateway-billing.md)
12:   flow — reading the credit balance and routing BYOK inference through the account's default AI
13:   Gateway.
14: - **Workers Observability:** gadgets can receive read-only access to logs, events, invocations,
15:   aggregate metrics, and traces either across an account or restricted to one Worker. Every result
16:   is authorized as an observation, and Worker bindings inject an immutable service filter and
17:   defensively discard foreign-service events. Distributed trace summaries are account-only because
18:   their names, timing, services, and counts describe the whole cross-service trace; a Worker binding
19:   can still retrieve its own events for a known trace ID.
20: 
21: Observability connections request `workers-observability.read`. The OAuth client must allow that
22: scope or Cloudflare will omit/reject it. Existing billing-only connections can add the grant when the
23: user first selects an observability resource. Cloudflare exposes account and Worker resource choices,
24: but both map to this one indivisible OAuth scope; resource bindings provide the finer capability
25: boundary after connection.
26: 
27: Workers telemetry is retained by Cloudflare for at most seven days. Queries default to the last hour,
28: and the Worker picker searches the full retention window. Suggested bindings are
29: `CLOUDFLARE_OBSERVABILITY` for account access and `WORKER_OBSERVABILITY` for one Worker.
30: 
31: ### Sharing a gadget that reads telemetry
32: 
33: A binding is not transferable. When a gadget with an observability binding is shared, each
34: collaborator is admitted only if **their own** connected Cloudflare account can read that resource
35: (`addObserver` checks it against their credentials, not the owner's). A collaborator without access is
36: refused, and a verification that fails for any other reason — a 5xx, a transport error — is also a
37: refusal rather than an admission.
38: 
39: ### What a Worker binding trusts, and what it re-checks
40: 
41: The scope filter is prepended to every query, but a filter the provider *accepted* is not evidence it
42: *applied* it — three separate behaviours here return wrong-but-plausible data with no error. So events
43: are re-filtered on the way out, and a single foreign event is treated as proof the filter was dropped:
44: the provider's `count` is withheld (it would be a count of the whole account's matching telemetry) and
45: the event is logged at `error`. `statistics` is kept, because it describes what our query cost rather
46: than how much matched, and callers are told to read it for cost.
47: 
48: The re-check is deliberately not a hard failure. The events returned are filtered and therefore safe,
49: and this provider has surprised us often enough that turning a hypothetical disclosure into a
50: guaranteed outage would be the worse trade.
51: 
52: `calculate()` is the exception, and knowingly so: an aggregate cannot be un-mixed, so there is no
53: second line of defence to add. It rests entirely on the injected filter. The fix that would work —
54: grouping by `$metadata.service` and keeping this binding's own group, whose value *is* the correctly
55: scoped answer even for a median — changes `limit` and `orderBy` semantics for every caller, so it is a
56: follow-up rather than a footnote.
57: 
58: ### Why discovery sometimes costs a query
59: 
60: Cloudflare's `telemetry/keys` and `telemetry/values` endpoints ignore the `filters` array they accept:
61: verified against a live account, they answer for the whole account no matter what is passed. A
62: Worker-scoped binding therefore cannot use them — they would disclose every field name and value in
63: the account. Whenever a discovery call has to be constrained (a Worker binding, or any caller-supplied
64: filter), the answer is derived instead from a filtered `telemetry/query` events sample, which the
65: provider does filter correctly. Unconstrained account-wide discovery still uses the cheap endpoints.
66: 
67: > Unresolved: whether the `workers-observability.read` scope alone is accepted, or whether Cloudflare
68: > requires the Workers Observability **Write** permission to read telemetry. This has not been
69: > verified against a live token; if reads 403 on a correctly-scoped grant, that is the first thing to
70: > check.
71: 
72: ### Two names for one field
73: 
74: A log's own structured fields are returned nested under `source` but are **indexed under their bare
75: name**: `logger.warn(msg, {event: "x"})` comes back as `source.event` and is queried as `event`.
76: Confirmed both ways — `telemetry/keys` on a live account reports `event`/`component`/`level` and no
77: `source.*` key at all, and the [Workers Logs
78: docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/observability/logs/workers-logs/) show
79: `console.log({user_id: 123})` being filtered as `user_id`.
80: 
81: This matters because the provider accepts an unknown filter key, matches nothing, and returns an empty
82: page with no error. So discovery reports indexed names (`observability-discovery.ts`), and
83: `observabilityFieldKey` additionally accepts a `source.`-prefixed key as an alias wherever a caller
84: names a field — filters, `calculations`, `groupBys`, `listValues` — because copying a path out of a
85: `listEvents` result is the obvious thing to do and used to fail silently.
86: 
87: `openid` is intentionally **not** requested — the Cloudflare dashboard OAuth client isn't permitted
88: that scope; identity comes from the `/user` API (`user-details.read`).
89: 
90: ### Why an error's text never reaches the log
91: 
92: `summarizeFilter` deliberately keeps filter *values* out of the audit trail — they are caller text.
93: But a provider error message can quote that same value straight back, so logging the message would
94: readmit through the error path exactly what the audit path excludes. `CloudflareObservabilityApiError`
95: therefore carries Cloudflare's numeric `codes` alongside the message: the request log names the
96: codes, and the message travels only to the caller who caused it.
97: 
98: The codes are not the discriminator, though — Cloudflare can return a message with no numeric code
99: at all, so the error records separately whether the message is *its* or *ours*, and only ours is
100: logged. A provider failure carrying no codes is therefore logged as a bare status, which is the
101: fail-closed answer: the status still says what happened without quoting anyone's filter back.
102: 
103: ### Listing accounts is a walk, not a request
104: 
105: `/accounts` is paginated and defaults to **20** per page, so a single GET silently returns a truncated
106: list — an account past the first page simply cannot be picked, with nothing to indicate why. The
107: account picker's substring match also stays client-side: `name` is the only documented server-side
108: filter and whether it matches exactly or by substring is not specified, so pushing it down would trade
109: a visible truncation for an invisible one.
110: 
111: ## Setting Up Cloudflare OAuth Credentials
112: 
113: You need a Cloudflare dashboard OAuth client (client id + secret). The dashboard OAuth endpoints and
114: scopes are hardcoded in `src/oauth.ts`, so you only configure the client id/secret and register the
115: redirect URI. Ensure the client's scope allowlist includes `workers-observability.read` when this
116: deployment offers Workers Observability resources.
117: 
118: ### Step 1: Register the redirect URI
119: 
120: The gatekeeper's OAuth redirect URI is:
121: 
122: ```
123: ${BASE_URL}/oauth
124: ```
125: 
126: where `BASE_URL` defaults to `http://localhost:8787/gatekeeper/cloudflare` in dev — i.e. the full
127: redirect URI is:
128: 
129: ```
130: http://localhost:8787/gatekeeper/cloudflare/oauth
131: ```
132: 
133: Register **exactly** this (replace the host with your `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` when not running locally) as
134: an allowed/pre-registered redirect URL on the Cloudflare OAuth client. If it isn't registered you'll
135: get an `invalid_request` error: _"the 'redirect_uri' parameter does not match any of the OAuth 2.0
136: Client's pre-registered redirect urls."_
137: 
138: ### Step 2: Configure Your Local Environment
139: 
140: Create a `.env` file in this package's directory (`packages/gatekeeper-cloudflare/.env`):
141: 
142: ```bash
143: CLIENT_ID=your-client-id-here
144: CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret-here
145: ```
146: 
147: In local dev, `run-dev-server.ts` will also seed these from `CLOUDFLARE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` /
148: `CLOUDFLARE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` if you'd rather set them in the root `.dev.vars`. A per-package
149: `.env` takes precedence and keeps the credential with the gatekeeper that uses it.
150: 
151: > **Note**: The `.env` file is gitignored and should never be committed.
152: 
153: ### Step 3: (Optional) Enable Cloudflare sign-in / billing
154: 
155: To offer "Continue with Cloudflare" on the login page, add `cloudflare` to the deployment's
156: `AUTH_GATEKEEPERS` allowlist (e.g. in the root `.dev.vars`):
157: 
158: ```
159: AUTH_GATEKEEPERS=cloudflare,google,github
160: ```
161: 
162: The order controls the order of the login buttons. For the AI Gateway billing / top-up flow, also
163: set `ENABLE_CLOUDFLARE_LIMITS=true` (see [AI Gateway billing](../../docs/ai-gateway-billing.md)); a
164: user enables billing by connecting Cloudflare, which requests the billing scopes
165: (`offline_access aig.read aig.run user-details.read account-settings.read`). Connecting all
166: Cloudflare gadget resources also requests `workers-observability.read`.
167: 
168: ### Step 4: Verify Setup
169: 
170: 1. Start the application in dev mode (see the root README.md).
171: 2. On the login page, click **Continue with Cloudflare**.
172: 3. A pop-up opens to the Cloudflare authorization page; approve it.
173: 4. The pop-up closes and you're signed in, identified by your Cloudflare account email.
174: 5. To use AI Gateway credits, open **Usage & billing** in settings and **Connect Cloudflare** (this
175:    requests billing scopes only).
176: 
177: ## Troubleshooting
178: 
179: ### "redirect_uri ... does not match any of the ... pre-registered redirect urls"
180: 
181: The redirect URI isn't registered on the OAuth client. Register exactly
182: `http://localhost:8787/gatekeeper/cloudflare/oauth` (or your `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` equivalent) — no
183: trailing slash, `http` not `https` for localhost.
184: 
185: ### "Not configured" page during authorization
186: 
187: `CLIENT_ID` / `CLIENT_SECRET` are missing. Ensure they're set (per-package `.env` or seeded from the
188: root `.dev.vars`), then restart the dev server.

(End of file - total 188 lines)
</content>

*applied* it — three separate behaviours here return wrong-but-plausible data with no error. So events

the provider's `count` is withheld (it would be a count of the whole account's matching telemetry) and
the event is logged at `error`. `statistics` is kept, because it describes what our query cost rather
than how much matched, and callers are told to read it for cost.

The re-check is deliberately not a hard failure. The events returned are filtered and therefore safe,
and this provider has surprised us often enough that turning a hypothetical disclosure into a
guaranteed outage would be the worse trade.

`calculate()` is the exception, and knowingly so: an aggregate cannot be un-mixed, so there is no
second line of defence to add. It rests entirely on the injected filter. The fix that would work —
grouping by `$metadata.service` and keeping this binding's own group, whose value *is* the correctly
scoped answer even for a median — changes `limit` and `orderBy` semantics for every caller, so it is a
follow-up rather than a footnote.

### Why discovery sometimes costs a query

Cloudflare's `telemetry/keys` and `telemetry/values` endpoints ignore the `filters` array they accept:
verified against a live account, they answer for the whole account no matter what is passed. A
Worker-scoped binding therefore cannot use them — they would disclose every field name and value in
the account. Whenever a discovery call has to be constrained (a Worker binding, or any caller-supplied
filter), the answer is derived instead from a filtered `telemetry/query` events sample, which the
provider does filter correctly. Unconstrained account-wide discovery still uses the cheap endpoints.

> Unresolved: whether the `workers-observability.read` scope alone is accepted, or whether Cloudflare
> requires the Workers Observability **Write** permission to read telemetry. This has not been
> verified against a live token; if reads 403 on a correctly-scoped grant, that is the first thing to
> check.

### Two names for one field

A log's own structured fields are returned nested under `source` but are **indexed under their bare
name**: `logger.warn(msg, {event: "x"})` comes back as `source.event` and is queried as `event`.
Confirmed both ways — `telemetry/keys` on a live account reports `event`/`component`/`level` and no
`source.*` key at all, and the [Workers Logs
docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/observability/logs/workers-logs/) show
`console.log({user_id: 123})` being filtered as `user_id`.

This matters because the provider accepts an unknown filter key, matches nothing, and returns an empty
page with no error. So discovery reports indexed names (`observability-discovery.ts`), and
`observabilityFieldKey` additionally accepts a `source.`-prefixed key as an alias wherever a caller
names a field — filters, `calculations`, `groupBys`, `listValues` — because copying a path out of a
`listEvents` result is the obvious thing to do and used to fail silently.

`openid` is intentionally **not** requested — the Cloudflare dashboard OAuth client isn't permitted
that scope; identity comes from the `/user` API (`user-details.read`).

### Why an error's text never reaches the log

`summarizeFilter` deliberately keeps filter *values* out of the audit trail — they are caller text.
But a provider error message can quote that same value straight back, so logging the message would
readmit through the error path exactly what the audit path excludes. `CloudflareObservabilityApiError`
therefore carries Cloudflare's numeric `codes` alongside the message: the request log names the
codes, and the message travels only to the caller who caused it.

The codes are not the discriminator, though — Cloudflare can return a message with no numeric code
at all, so the error records separately whether the message is *its* or *ours*, and only ours is
logged. A provider failure carrying no codes is therefore logged as a bare status, which is the
fail-closed answer: the status still says what happened without quoting anyone's filter back.

### Listing accounts is a walk, not a request

`/accounts` is paginated and defaults to **20** per page, so a single GET silently returns a truncated
list — an account past the first page simply cannot be picked, with nothing to indicate why. The
account picker's substring match also stays client-side: `name` is the only documented server-side
filter and whether it matches exactly or by substring is not specified, so pushing it down would trade
a visible truncation for an invisible one.

## Setting Up Cloudflare OAuth Credentials

You need a Cloudflare dashboard OAuth client (client id + secret). The dashboard OAuth endpoints and
scopes are hardcoded in `src/oauth.ts`, so you only configure the client id/secret and register the
redirect URI. Ensure the client's scope allowlist includes `workers-observability.read` when this
deployment offers Workers Observability resources.

### Step 1: Register the redirect URI

The gatekeeper's OAuth redirect URI is:

```
${BASE_URL}/oauth
```

where `BASE_URL` defaults to `http://localhost:8787/gatekeeper/cloudflare` in dev — i.e. the full
redirect URI is:

```
http://localhost:8787/gatekeeper/cloudflare/oauth
```

Register **exactly** this (replace the host with your `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` when not running locally) as
an allowed/pre-registered redirect URL on the Cloudflare OAuth client. If it isn't registered you'll
get an `invalid_request` error: _"the 'redirect_uri' parameter does not match any of the OAuth 2.0
Client's pre-registered redirect urls."_

### Step 2: Configure Your Local Environment

Create a `.env` file in this package's directory (`packages/gatekeeper-cloudflare/.env`):

```bash
CLIENT_ID=your-client-id-here
CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret-here
```

In local dev, `run-dev-server.ts` will also seed these from `CLOUDFLARE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` /
`CLOUDFLARE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` if you'd rather set them in the root `.dev.vars`. A per-package
`.env` takes precedence and keeps the credential with the gatekeeper that uses it.

> **Note**: The `.env` file is gitignored and should never be committed.

### Step 3: (Optional) Enable Cloudflare sign-in / billing

To offer "Continue with Cloudflare" on the login page, add `cloudflare` to the deployment's
`AUTH_GATEKEEPERS` allowlist (e.g. in the root `.dev.vars`):

```
AUTH_GATEKEEPERS=cloudflare,google,github
```

The order controls the order of the login buttons. For the AI Gateway billing / top-up flow, also
set `ENABLE_CLOUDFLARE_LIMITS=true` (see [AI Gateway billing](../../docs/ai-gateway-billing.md)); a
user enables billing by connecting Cloudflare, which requests the billing scopes
(`offline_access aig.read aig.run user-details.read account-settings.read`). Connecting all
Cloudflare gadget resources also requests `workers-observability.read`.

### Step 4: Verify Setup

1. Start the application in dev mode (see the root README.md).
2. On the login page, click **Continue with Cloudflare**.
3. A pop-up opens to the Cloudflare authorization page; approve it.
4. The pop-up closes and you're signed in, identified by your Cloudflare account email.
5. To use AI Gateway credits, open **Usage & billing** in settings and **Connect Cloudflare** (this
   requests billing scopes only).

## Troubleshooting

### "redirect_uri ... does not match any of the ... pre-registered redirect urls"

The redirect URI isn't registered on the OAuth client. Register exactly
`http://localhost:8787/gatekeeper/cloudflare/oauth` (or your `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` equivalent) — no
trailing slash, `http` not `https` for localhost.

### "Not configured" page during authorization

`CLIENT_ID` / `CLIENT_SECRET` are missing. Ensure they're set (per-package `.env` or seeded from the
root `.dev.vars`), then restart the dev server.

1: // Derives indexed field names and values from telemetry events.
2: //
3: // Why this exists: Cloudflare's `/telemetry/keys` and `/telemetry/values` endpoints ignore the
4: // `filters` they are sent. That was verified against the live API — a `$metadata.service eq <other>`
5: // filter still returns this account's other services, and the same filter on `/telemetry/query`
6: // correctly returns nothing. So on a single-Worker binding those two endpoints cannot be constrained
7: // at the provider, and a naive discovery call would hand an agent every Worker's field values.
8: //
9: // Deriving from a service-filtered events sample is correct by construction: the events have already
10: // passed both the provider's filter and this module's own scope filter, so nothing another Worker
11: // emitted can appear in the result.
12:

15:   CloudflareObservabilityKey,
16:   CloudflareObservabilityValue,
17:   CloudflareObservabilityValueType,
18: } from "./types.js";

20: type Primitive = string | number | boolean;

22: // How each container in the response envelope maps onto the name a field is actually *indexed* under.
23: // `$metadata` and `$workers` are addressed by their dotted path, but the caller's own structured log
24: // payload is not: Cloudflare indexes `console.log({event: "x"})` under the bare name `event` and only
25: // nests it beneath `source` when returning it. Verified against the live `/telemetry/keys`, which
26: // reports `event`/`component`/`level` and no `source.*` key at all, and documented under "Logging
27: // structured JSON objects" in
28: // https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/observability/logs/workers-logs/.
29: //
30: // Discovery therefore has to report the filterable name, not the envelope path. Reporting
31: // `source.event` was a silent trap: the provider accepts an unknown key, matches nothing, and returns
32: // an empty page with no error, so an agent filtering on a field it had just discovered got zero
33: // results after scanning the whole timeframe.
34: const INDEXED_NAMESPACES: ReadonlyArray<{
35:   container: "$metadata" | "$workers" | "source";
36:   prefix: string;
37: }> = [
38:   { container: "$metadata", prefix: "$metadata" },
39:   { container: "$workers", prefix: "$workers" },
40:   { container: "source", prefix: "" },
41: ];

43: // Bounds the walk of an arbitrarily deep user-authored `source` payload.
44: const MAX_FIELD_DEPTH = 6;

46: /** Joins a field path, treating an unprefixed namespace's empty prefix as no leading segment. */
47: function fieldPath(prefix: string, name: string): string {
48:   return prefix === "" ? name : `${prefix}.${name}`;

53:     // An unprefixed namespace whose container is itself a scalar has no field name to report.

58:   if (depth >= MAX_FIELD_DEPTH || !value || typeof value !== "object" || Array.isArray(value)) return;

3: //

5: // own properties on an `RpcTarget`. Each is a one-line delegate to `callTool`, so the scope check,
6: // approval queue, and observation record stay in one place and the delegates inherit the

9: import type { ClassifiedTool } from "./tools.js";

11: /**
12:  * Method names that must never be generated. The first group is measured: an `RpcStub` intercepts
13:  * these or resolves them to something other than the target's method, so a tool named after one
14:  * would appear to exist and then misbehave. The second is the session's own surface.
15:  */
16: export const RESERVED_METHOD_NAMES: ReadonlySet<string> = new Set([
17:   // Intercepted or hijacked by the RPC stub itself.
18:   "then", "catch", "finally", "dup", "onRpcBroken", "constructor", "toString", "valueOf",
19:   "hasOwnProperty", "__proto__", "map",
20:   // The session's own methods.
21:   "callTool", "getActionResult", "listTools",
22: ]);
23: 
24: /**
25:  * Converts an MCP tool name to a JavaScript method name: `list_issues` -> `listIssues`. Null when
26:  * the name cannot become a usable identifier; servers are free to name tools anything.
27:  */
28: export function toMethodName(wireName: string): string | null {
29:   const parts = wireName.split(/[^A-Za-z0-9]+/).filter(part => part.length > 0);
30:   if (parts.length === 0) return null;
31: 
32:   const [first, ...rest] = parts;
33:   const name = first[0].toLowerCase() + first.slice(1) +
34:     rest.map(part => part[0].toUpperCase() + part.slice(1)).join("");
35: 
36:   // A leading digit cannot start an identifier, and a name the agent cannot type in the generated
37:   // `.d.ts` is not worth having. Such tools remain reachable through `callTool`.
38:   return /^[A-Za-z_$]/.test(name) ? name : null;
39: }

43:  * collision are dropped: with `list_issues` and `listIssues` both published, one shadowing the other

47:   const claims = new Map<string, string[]>();

51:     const existing = claims.get(method);

1: // Matching a text query against a tool, shared by every catalog search.
2: //
3: // One implementation on purpose. Two connectors search the same way over different sources -- one
4: // filters definitions already in hand, while endpoint discovery applies it as each page is parsed --
5: // and a query answered differently depending on the path would be a difference nobody asked for and
6: // nobody could see.
7: 
8: import type { McpTool } from "./client.js";
9: 
10: /** Longest accepted agent-supplied search query. */
11: export const MAX_QUERY_CHARS = 200;
12: 
13: /** Most tool summaries returned by one search. */
14: export const MAX_SEARCH_RESULTS = 20;
15: 
16: // Longest run of one server-supplied field considered when matching.
17: //
18: // The bound is load-bearing on the path that matches tools as they arrive from the endpoint, before
19: // per-field clamping: a description there is whatever the server sent, and every term is tested
20: // against it. Applied unconditionally rather than only on that path, so no caller has to know which
21: // of its inputs were already clamped in order to be safe.
22: const MAX_SEARCHABLE_FIELD_CHARS = 4000;
23: 
24: // Normalizes text for matching. Word separators become spaces so that a query typed as
25: // `list issues`, `list_issues`, or `listIssues` reaches a tool named `github_list_issues`: MCP tool
26: // names are overwhelmingly snake_case or camelCase, and a portal prefixes each with `{server_id}_`,
27: // so leaving word boundaries in place would make the obvious query miss the obvious tool.
28: function normalize(text: string): string {
29:   return text.slice(0, MAX_SEARCHABLE_FIELD_CHARS)
30:     .replace(/([a-z0-9])([A-Z])/g, "$1 $2")
31:     .toLowerCase()
32:     .replace(/[_\-\s]+/g, " ");
33: }
34: 
35: /** Splits a query into normalized terms that a matching tool must all contain. */
36: export function toolQueryTerms(query: string): string[] {
37:   return [...new Set(normalize(query.slice(0, MAX_QUERY_CHARS)).split(" ").filter(Boolean))];
38: }
39: 
40: /** Returns whether a tool's name, title, and description collectively match every term. */
41: export function matchesToolQuery(
42:   tool: Pick<McpTool, "name" | "title" | "description">,
43:   terms: readonly string[],
44: ): boolean {
45:   if (terms.length === 0) return false;
46:   const text = [tool.name, tool.title, tool.description]
47:     .filter((value): value is string => typeof value === "string")
48:     .map(normalize)
49:     .join(" ");
50:   return terms.every(term => text.includes(term));
